summary:
Andorra's legal gender recognition framework rests on the Family Law of 21 July 2022, which allows trans people to change the name and gender recorded on legal documents through a simple administrative process that requires no medical intervention. Adoption has been open to same-sex couples since the 2014 civil union law, so a trans visitor in a relationship that Andorran law reads through birth-sex status can expect the same partnership recognition as other couples.

Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender identity and expression in employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments, and extends that protection to education settings. Law 14/2019 of the same date on the rights of children and adolescents requires that transgender children be respected in their gender identity. Offences motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract additional penalties beyond the base offence.

Enforcement of the bias-crime framework is incomplete. Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month during 2025, a figure covering all bias motives rather than trans complaints alone and reported without any population denominator. DiversAnd logged incidents during the June Pride period and has called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so that it can be prosecuted as hate crime; no such classification system was in place. The Ministry of Equality ran equality measures during the year.

The head of government, Xavier Espot Zamora, has held office since 2019 and came out as gay in September 2023; he remains the serving prime minister.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791, and the age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships.
tangentialFactors:
A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September 2023 was taken down online with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal; the print edition had already circulated.

Andorra has an organised LGBT presence dating to the first demonstration on 6 September 2002 and the first pride parade on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. That association ended its work in 2018; DiversAnd formed in 2019 and held a pride parade that June. On 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality released the short film #lovingdiversity to raise awareness online.
localsOnly:
Gender-affirming care for adolescents was still under negotiation in 2023: DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health in August to press for protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds and, in some cases, 14-year-olds, following the 2022 regulatory changes. DiversAnd also works on bullying and discrimination in schools.

Documented risks to LGBT young people include the murder of Nuno Ribeiro, a 17-year-old gay man killed in 2000 because of his sexual orientation, which prompted public outcry, and reports of parents expelling children from the home over their sexual orientation. No general homicide or crime rate for Andorra is available, so these cannot be placed against a background rate.
outOfScopeNotes:
GayLawNet's Andorra page carries a limited-information marking and cites Penal Code Article 206 for the age of consent, while other sources cite Articles 162 and 163; the article numbering is unresolved.

The bias-incident figure of two to three per month is a raw count with no population denominator and no breakdown by motive, and because no formal registration and classification system exists it is not a classified hate-crime count. Whether it understates or overstates the level of anti-trans violence cannot be determined from the available material.

The review material covers calendar years 2023 and 2025; no data for 2024 was available.
